title: Yemen’s Houthis renew threat against Riyadh airport as flights set to resume
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis renewed threats against Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, warning airlines and travellers to avoid the facility as it prepares to resume limited operations.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a military target and warned that attacks against the facility would continue, Reuters reported.
The warning came hours after King Khalid International Airport announced plans to reopen two terminals following a suspension of operations earlier this month.
Under the revised arrangements, Terminal 1 will handle domestic flights, while Terminal 2 will serve international flights operated by Saudi national carriers, beginning Sunday.
Airport operations were suspended on October 10 after a Houthi-claimed attack killed 13 people and injured more than 300 others.
The assault was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade, prompting authorities to extend the airport’s closure two days later.
The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones, including airports, ports and oil facilities, as regional hostilities intensify.
The attacks have placed Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally and major global oil exporter, under growing pressure amid the wider regional conflict.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has escalated its military involvement in Yemen, launching airstrikes against Houthi positions and supporting a government counteroffensive.
The renewed campaign follows the Houthis’ seizure of strategic territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month, further intensifying fighting between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned group.

title: Meta’s capital-raising plans expose a major weakness in the AI boom
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Meta's (NASDAQ:META) recent surprise move to issue a new class of non-voting stock has weighed on sentiment toward the AI giant, as Thursday's 7% sell-off shows despite strong earnings. But one of its motives for the move paints a more concerning picture for the AI-dependent stock market.
In its filing, Meta's special committee highlighted that a motivation for the decision was not only to keep CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California but also "an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital," citing recent large capital raises and anticipated capital raises at Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI "to fund the same AI growth."
"The Special Committee considered that, while the Company presently has sufficient capital resources for its current needs, in order to finance its funding needs going forward it would be prudent for the Company to do so before even more companies have absorbed available capital in the market," the filing said.
Meta expects to use the new Class C shares for equity offerings from time to time, subject to market conditions, and wants them available as early as the end of 2026.
The language is striking because it suggests that even one of the world's most profitable technology companies sees access to capital as something that could become increasingly constrained as the AI arms race intensifies.
Meta is hardly a company in immediate financial distress. But its filing makes clear that the scale of investment required to compete in AI is changing its financing calculus. The new shares would give it another way to raise money, compensate employees and finance acquisitions without diluting the voting power of existing shareholders.
That flexibility could prove valuable as the company commits ever-larger sums to AI infrastructure. More importantly, however, Meta's reasoning raises a broader question for investors: What happens if the companies racing to dominate AI begin competing not just for computing power, but for the capital needed to finance the race itself?
The AI spending race is becoming a race for capital
The companies competing to dominate AI are embarking on an extraordinary investment cycle. Building and operating increasingly powerful models requires vast computing infrastructure, including specialized chips, data centers, networking equipment and electricity. Those investments must be financed well before their eventual returns are fully established.
Meta has raised its projected 2026 capital expenditure to between $135 billion and $145 billion, underscoring the scale of the investment required to sustain its AI ambitions. Its third-quarter results showed revenue growth of 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, but capital expenditures, including finance lease repayments, reached $34.91 billion. Free cash flow turned negative as spending outpaced cash generated after investment.
Those figures do not mean Meta cannot finance its ambitions through its existing business. Its advertising operations remain a significant source of cash. But they illustrate why the company may want additional financing options as its investment requirements expand.
Meta's filing explicitly identifies Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI as companies whose recent or anticipated capital raises could make the funding environment more challenging. The concern is not simply that Meta needs money. It is that many of the companies pursuing the same technological opportunity may need substantial amounts of money at the same time.
This creates a potential paradox for the industry. The greater the perceived opportunity in AI, the more aggressively companies may invest to capture it. But as more businesses seek financing for similar ambitions, competition for investor capital can intensify, potentially increasing the cost of funding and making it harder for some companies to finance their plans on attractive terms.
The risk is not necessarily that the money disappears overnight. Rather, the terms on which it is available could become less favorable just as companies feel compelled to spend more.
Why Meta wants another financing option
Meta's decision also highlights the distinction between having sufficient resources today and being able to fund a long-term investment strategy at an acceptable cost.
The new Class C shares are designed to separate economic ownership from voting power. Under the proposed arrangement, shareholders will receive non-voting shares alongside their existing stock, effectively creating a two-for-one stock distribution. Meta will then have a class of shares it can use for future equity offerings, employee compensation and acquisitions without reducing Zuckerberg's voting control.
That distinction is important because Zuckerberg controls a majority of Meta's voting power despite owning a much smaller share of its economic value. Issuing additional voting shares could weaken his control, while repurchasing shares to offset dilution consumes cash that could otherwise go toward AI investment.
The new structure gives Meta more flexibility to raise equity without forcing that trade-off. It could sell shares to investors, including large institutional or strategic investors, while preserving the governance arrangement that keeps Zuckerberg firmly in control.
Equity financing also has an advantage over borrowing: it does not create interest payments or contractual repayment obligations. But it is not cost-free. Issuing shares dilutes existing investors' economic ownership, and the value of that dilution depends on the price at which the shares are sold and the returns generated by the money raised.
For shareholders, preserving voting control is not the same as preserving economic value. Investors will still need to assess whether the returns generated by AI investments justify the capital committed to them and any dilution that follows.
Meta's move therefore has two implications. It gives the company another tool to finance its AI ambitions, but it also signals that management wants to prepare for a future in which those ambitions may require more outside capital.
A warning sign for the wider AI trade?
The broader concern is what Meta's disclosure might reveal about the financing conditions underpinning the AI boom.
The market has largely focused on the enormous spending commitments being made by major technology companies and the potential revenue that AI could eventually generate. Less attention has been paid to what happens if the companies pursuing those opportunities begin competing more directly for a finite pool of investment capital.
Meta's filing provides an unusually explicit acknowledgment of that possibility from a company at the center of the AI investment cycle. Its special committee is concerned that other companies could absorb available capital before Meta has secured the funding it may need in the years ahead.
That is not proof that capital is running out, or that investors are about to abandon AI. The pool of potential financing is not fixed. Companies can generate cash internally, issue bonds, sell equity, bring in private investors or form partnerships to fund infrastructure. Capital raised by one company does not automatically prevent another from raising money.
Still, those alternatives are not interchangeable. Debt increases financial obligations, equity can dilute shareholders, and private financing or infrastructure partnerships can come with their own costs and constraints. If the industry requires ever-larger sums to sustain its growth, the cost and availability of financing could become as important as the amount being spent.
The implications could extend beyond the companies raising money directly. If investors become less willing to finance ambitious AI projects, private companies could face pressure to delay expansion, while publicly traded companies might have to reassess capital expenditure plans or accept less favorable financing terms. A more selective funding environment could also expose differences between companies with strong cash-generating businesses and those more dependent on external capital.
For investors, the concern is therefore less about an imminent funding crisis than about the possibility that financing becomes more expensive or restrictive just as expectations for AI-driven growth become more demanding.
The real test is whether AI spending generates sufficient returns
Ultimately, the sustainability of the AI boom will depend on whether the revenues and profits generated by the technology can justify the infrastructure being built to support it.
If AI adoption produces durable new revenue streams, boosts productivity and supports attractive returns on invested capital, the industry's enormous funding requirements may prove justified. Companies that secure financing early could be well positioned to capitalize on the opportunity.
If monetization falls short of expectations, however, the same spending commitments could become a burden. Companies might find themselves competing for capital to sustain projects whose returns take longer to materialize than anticipated. That could pressure valuations, constrain investment elsewhere and expose investors to the consequences of an industry-wide rush to build capacity.
There is also a potential feedback loop. As companies spend more to keep pace with competitors, investors may demand stronger evidence that those expenditures will generate sufficient returns. If the evidence fails to materialize quickly enough, the market could become more selective about which companies deserve continued access to capital. That, in turn, could force some businesses to slow their investment just as competitors continue to expand.
Such a scenario would not necessarily mean the AI opportunity itself is overstated. It would mean that the financial returns from the technology may be distributed unevenly, and that some companies could struggle to finance their ambitions even as others succeed.
Meta's new share class does not establish that such a reckoning is approaching. But its filing reveals that the company sees a strategic advantage in securing financing flexibility before its competitors absorb more of the available capital.
For a market that has spent years pricing in the transformative potential of AI, that is an important distinction. The next phase of the boom may depend not only on who builds the most powerful technology, but also on who can finance the race — and generate enough returns to make the spending worthwhile.

title: Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, make arrests
full_text:
By Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira
LISBON, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Portuguese police cleared a housing protest camp from the centre of Lisbon in the early hours of Sunday, charging demonstrators and making several arrests, with minor injuries reported, though figures were not immediately available.
Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit.
"We have an obligation to fight for what we believe in," said one marcher, Vitor Gomes, 21, a multimedia communications student, adding that housing speculation, wealth concentration and rising inequality made him pessimistic about the future.
Shortly after 2 a.m., dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square, after warning protesters to remove their tents or face their dismantling, and threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted.
Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of the capital’s main avenues.
Hundreds gathered to protect the encampment after police dismantled a similar camp there on Tuesday.
The police action was "completely disproportionate", however, as there had been no public disorder, Left Bloc lawmaker Fabian Figueiredo said before the action.
"The worst thing that could happen tonight was having this police force charge hundreds of people who are here peacefully. Why?" asked Figueiredo, who was at the camp.
Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent, with young people among those hardest hit.
The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.
The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.
The protest followed similar demonstrations in Belgium, France, Italy and Spain.

title: Trump touts $4 billion Audi plant in Georgia as he defends tariffs
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- U.S. President Donald Trump defended his tariff policies during a campaign rally in Georgia on Saturday, announcing that Volkswagen (ETR) plans to build a new Audi manufacturing plant in the state.
Trump said the investment demonstrated how tariffs were encouraging foreign manufacturers to expand production in the United States.
The proposed facility, valued at approximately $4 billion by Audi, is expected to create 4,500 jobs and produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually.
Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with production targeted for the early 2030s.
Audi plans to manufacture its larger premium sport utility vehicles at the Macon, Georgia, facility, including the Q7, Q8 and Q9 models.
Audi Chief Executive Gernot Döllner, who joined Trump at the rally, described the project as a long-term commitment to the U.S. automotive market.
Volkswagen also plans to expand its Scout Motors facility under construction in South Carolina, adding capacity for another 25,000 vehicles annually.
Trump credited his administration’s trade policies for securing the investment, arguing that the project would not have materialised without tariffs.
The announcement comes as the president faces mounting political pressure over inflation and household living costs ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Higher energy prices linked to the Iran war have added to consumer concerns, complicating the administration’s efforts to highlight manufacturing investments.
Trump’s Georgia appearance was his second campaign visit to the state in two weeks as Republicans attempt to unseat Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff.
Republican challenger Mike Collins trails Ossoff by more than eight percentage points in the RealClearPolitics polling average.
The Cook Political Report currently rates the Senate contest as likely Democratic, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans despite the administration’s latest manufacturing investment announcement.

title: How should investors think about GTA VI pre-order performance?
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Investors should avoid relying on Grand Theft Auto VI pre-orders to gauge overall demand, Goldman Sachs said, arguing that changing purchasing habits could make early sales figures misleading ahead of the game’s November 19 release.
In an October 19 research report, the investment bank highlighted the growing importance of digital distribution, which has fundamentally changed how consumers purchase major video game releases.
GTA VI has recorded more than six million pre-orders across PlayStation and Xbox since June 25, according to third-party data.
However, digital purchases now account for more than 85% of Take-Two Interactive’s implied download bookings, reducing the need for customers to reserve copies months before launch.
Unlike GTA V’s 2013 release, when physical copies dominated sales, unlimited digital availability allows players to delay purchases until closer to launch.
Purchasing activity could accelerate around November 12, when players are expected to begin pre-loading the game.
Meanwhile, alternative demand indicators suggest considerable anticipation for the upcoming release.
Google search interest in September was approximately 50% higher than comparable pre-launch levels for GTA V, while an extended trailer released through Netflix attracted more than 31 million views within four days.
These engagement trends suggest GTA VI could become one of the biggest AAA gaming releases in history.
Current projections indicate approximately 34 million units could be sold during Take-Two’s fiscal 2027, generating around $1.9 billion in implied download bookings.
The estimates assume a standard edition price of $79.99 and a 30% distribution fee.
The potential market includes more than 125 million PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S users, leaving room for stronger-than-expected sales.
Premium editions could provide additional revenue upside, although their share of purchases may decline as casual players enter the market.
Take-Two Interactive (NASDAQ) retains a Buy rating and a $285 price target, implying approximately 39% upside from the report’s reference price of $205.28.
Post-launch sales figures will provide a clearer indication of GTA VI’s commercial performance than early pre-order trends.

title: Obama unloads on Trump while stumping for Democrats ahead of midterms
full_text:
By Dan Catchpole
Oct 24 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday one of his Democratic predecessors did just that.
Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations.
Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration. Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the November 3 vote as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump’s presidency.
"We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government," Obama said.
Obama, president from 2009 until Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative.
The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats’ frequently repeated criticisms of Trump and of Republicans’ willingness to go along with him.
"We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this," Obama said. "Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this ... Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found that 63% of Americans think the president and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings.
Obama also ridiculed the administration’s claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters.
"Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world," Obama said.
The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasizing unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth someone "laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops" and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky.
"He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama said.

title: HSBC sees cautious optimism in VC and PE activity
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Venture capital (VC) and private equity (PE) investors are cautiously optimistic about near-term dealmaking, although confidence in the longer-term outlook has weakened, according to a new HSBC survey.
HSBC’s latest Funding the Future Survey found that 48% of private investors expect VC and PE activity to increase over the next quarter, up from 44% in July.
However, expectations for growth over the next 12 months declined to 54% from 64%, with the deterioration concentrated in Asia Pacific.
Deal valuations have improved, with 51% of respondents reporting that recent financings were predominantly up rounds, the highest reading in the survey’s history.
Only 3% reported mostly down rounds, suggesting that the valuation adjustments experienced during 2022 and 2023 have largely worked through the market.
Artificial intelligence remains the dominant investment theme, with 85% of respondents identifying AI as the sector most likely to attract private capital in the coming quarter.
Nevertheless, concerns about AI infrastructure spending are increasing.
Some 56% of investors expect a meaningful slowdown in AI infrastructure investment within six to 12 months, compared with 51% previously.
The proportion considering such a slowdown very likely nearly doubled to 20% from 11%.
Data centre real estate and colocation providers are now viewed as the most vulnerable segment, cited by 55% of respondents, up from 24% in July.
Meanwhile, 29% of investors said they would reduce AI exposure by a quarter if their identified downside scenario materialised, compared with 7% previously.
Exit intentions have reached a survey high, with 85% planning to exit at least one portfolio company within 12 months.
Trade sales remain the preferred exit strategy at 73%, while interest in initial public offerings has risen to 35%. Mergers have also gained traction, climbing to 31% from 17%.
Buyout preferences declined to 35% from 46%, reflecting concerns about borrowing costs.

title: Chinese equities face prolonged downturn as earnings forecasts tumble
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Chinese stocks face mounting pressure as weakening corporate earnings threaten to prolong a selloff that has wiped $3.5 trillion from the country’s equity market since May.
The downturn pushed China’s CSI 300 Index into a bear market last week, while Hong Kong technology shares approached levels that would erase gains made since Beijing’s major stimulus package two years ago.
Weak consumer spending and intense corporate competition have squeezed profit margins across industries, including banking, electric vehicles and artificial intelligence.
Consensus 2026 earnings estimates for companies in the MSCI China Index have fallen more than 4% since March.
Profit forecasts for the Hang Seng Tech Index have declined over 13% during the same period.
Companies reporting third-quarter results have missed earnings expectations by an average of 9%, putting the index on course for its second-worst quarterly performance against forecasts in two years.
Battery manufacturer CATL reported disappointing quarterly profits, while China Mobile recorded an 8% decline in net income for the first nine months of 2026.
Ganfeng Lithium also missed earnings expectations amid falling commodity prices.
Alibaba (NYSE) has meanwhile sought additional funding for artificial intelligence investments, including a $10 billion share offering that diluted existing shareholders.
Investor confidence has weakened further, with mainland trading volumes near their lowest levels since July 2025 and margin financing falling to a one-year low.
Chinese authorities have deployed state-backed investment funds to stabilise equities, although investors remain sceptical about the prospect of substantial economic stimulus.
China’s economy expanded 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, keeping growth within the government’s annual target range of 4.5% to 5%.
However, some institutional investors have adopted a cautiously optimistic stance, arguing that valuations remain reasonable and lower bond yields could encourage equity investment.

title: Sydney’s new international airport opens to passengers
full_text:
SYDNEY, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Sydney’s new A$5.6 billion ($3.94 billion) airport opened to passengers on Sunday after more than a decade of planning, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was a milestone for the country’s most populous city.
The new Western Sydney International Airport in Badgerys Creek, about 60 km (37.3 miles) west of central Sydney, will operate 24 hours a day, giving airlines access to a fast-growing and ethnically diverse population centre.
The current airport, located closer to Sydney’s central business district, can host takeoffs and landings only until 11 p.m. and after 6 a.m., limiting airline scheduling options relative to other major Australian cities like Melbourne.
"For the first time in more than 50 years, Australia is opening a major new airport. It’s a milestone that has been decades in the making," Albanese said in a statement.
"I’m very proud to officially open it," he said.
Qantas’ budget arm Jetstar was due to operate the first outbound flight to the Gold Coast on Sunday, the airport said in a statement. The airport has capacity for more than 80 million passenger movements annually, it said.
The start of passenger services comes after cargo flights commenced at the facility in July.
Located on a 1,780-hectare (4,398-acre) site purchased by the federal government in the 1980s, the airport was completed in July 2025 after a seven-year build and 15 years of planning.
($1 = 1.4219 Australian dollars)

title: 5 big analyst AI moves: ’Uniquely catalyst-rich’ months ahead for SpaceX
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Here are the biggest analyst moves in the area of artificial intelligence (AI) for this week.
Loop Capital downgrades Apple after supply chain checks reveal no iPhone recovery plan
Brokerage firm Loop Capital this week downgraded Apple to Hold from Buy and cut its price target to $330 from $370, after supply chain checks revealed Apple has no plans to recover the 13 million iPhone shipments cut in the second half of 2026.
Analyst Ananda Baruah said Apple previously reduced September- and December-quarter iPhone shipments by 10%, with Loop having initially believed those units could be made up through 2027 as the reductions were supply-related rather than demand-driven.
"This no longer appears to be the case," Baruah wrote.
Loop lowered its December-quarter iPhone unit forecast to 79 million from the Street’s 85 million, cutting its average selling price (ASP) estimate to $1,123 from $1,239. For calendar 2027, it raised its unit forecast to 260 million but cut ASP to $1,096 from $1,235, lowering iPhone revenue to $285 billion from $315 billion and trimming EPS to $9.76 from $10.11.
The broker also flagged potential gross margin risk as memory costs keep rising, lowering its normalized EPS estimate to $11 from $12 and applying Apple’s median P/E of 30 times to arrive at the new target.
"We continue to like AAPL’s longer-term share gain and Services story… but believe the stock also requires a fundamental catalyst reset after its recent stock appreciation," Baruah said.
JPMorgan upgrades Intel as pullback from peak makes risk-reward more balanced
JPMorgan has upgraded Intel to Neutral from Underweight, saying the risk/reward is now much more balanced as the stock approaches the bank’s $85 price target after pulling back roughly 40% from its June peak, compared with a 20-25% decline for the broader chip group.
Analyst Harlan Sur noted that since JPMorgan downgraded the stock in November 2022, Intel’s server x86 CPU revenue share has fallen from 77% to 53% and its PC CPU share from 81% to 68%, with a few more quarters of share losses expected, particularly in server CPUs.
In foundry, Intel appears to be making strong inroads on yields and new customer engagements, though it generated barely $1 billion in annualized external foundry revenue in the first half of 2026, compared with $150 billion for TSMC.
Sur said that since Lip Bu Tan became CEO, execution has improved in Intel’s core client and data center compute markets and in next-generation manufacturing. "Despite near-term concerns on AI infrastructure spending sustainability, we believe increasing agentic AI workloads (CPU intensive) and a very tight supply chain for leading edge silicon should drive continued positive EPS revisions in the upcoming earnings season and through CY27," he wrote.
JPMorgan’s 2028 EPS estimates sit about 15% above consensus.
"Risk/reward is more balanced at current levels and we move to a Neutral rating," Sur said.
Citi opens positive Catalyst Watch on SpaceX, sees coming months as "uniquely catalyst-rich"
Earlier in the week, Citi opened a positive 90-day Catalyst Watch on SpaceX, arguing the coming months will be "uniquely catalyst rich," after the company reported revenue that more than doubled in the third quarter and posted net income of $4.4 billion, its first profitable quarter as a public company.
Growth was driven largely by SpaceX’s AI segment, with space and connectivity businesses also expanding. CEO Elon Musk also offered some of his most detailed comments yet on a potential merger with Tesla, saying the move would be "a good idea" and confirming for the first time that special committees had been formed to discuss a potential union.
Musk said he expects annual recurring revenue (ARR) to reach between $500 billion and $1 trillion by end-2027, driven by surging demand for data-center space amid the AI boom.
Citi, which rates the stock Buy, pointed to six factors behind its positive catalyst watch: SpaceX’s "track record of beats/raises" expected to continue into the fourth quarter; Flight 15 as "a monumental space-industry catalyst that sets the stage for rapid reusability on a scale never before demonstrated in launch"; dollar-per-watt economics "trending significantly above consensus expectations"; an accelerated Grok model release cadence; the possibility of more detail on SpaceX’s power-generation solutions before year-end; and further clarity on its "evolving mobile strategy."
"We’ve described Buy-rated SPCX as being in the midst of a catalyst-rich 2-3 year arc, and we see the next 2-3 months in particular as uniquely catalyst rich even within that timeline that supports our positive investment thesis," Citi analysts said.
Buy Lam Research on pullback, Mizuho says
Mizuho has reiterated its Outperform rating on Lam Research and recommended buying the stock after a significant pullback following quarterly results, trimming its price target to $360 from $365.
Analyst Vijay Rakesh highlighted that Lam expects wafer fab equipment (WFE) spending to grow more than 29% in 2027 to over $200 billion, after rising about 42% to roughly $155 billion this year. "We are buyers on the pullback, as new greenfield fabs, NAND/HBM/Terafab position for upside," he wrote, also flagging Tesla’s comments pointing to "10s of $B WFE" from Terafab in early 2028 and $100 billion long-term.
Mizuho highlighted the emergence of SLC NAND as a major tailwind, with each 1 percentage point mix shift requiring 2% more NAND wafer capacity — a market where Lam holds about 90% share. NAND revenue rose 38% in the September quarter and foundry grew 28%. The broker estimates Lam’s revenue will grow 37% next year, ahead of 30% consensus, and believes Lam sees 10 new tier 1 fabs coming online in 2027.
"We see LRCX well positioned with: 1) wide competitive moats, 2) secular technology trends with HPC/AI/ML, HBM/CoWoS/TSV, GAA/BPD, and 3) rising capital intensity at the leading edge," Rakesh said.
Lam reported September-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion and EPS of $2.20, broadly in line with consensus, with gross margin rising 40 basis points sequentially to 52.4%. December-quarter guidance of $8.6 billion in revenue and EPS of $2.33 came in slightly above expectations.
AI bubble exists but will not burst yet: Yardeni
This week, Financial research firm Yardeni Research introduced an AI Bubble Meter, built using Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, which it says confirms a bubble exists in AI-related stocks but shows it is not yet close to bursting.
The tool has two dials. The Conditions dial measures whether a bubble exists by drawing on the setups that preceded the 1999-2000 tech bust and the 2006-2007 housing bust, and currently reads 83 out of 100. The Triggers dial tracks whether the forces that ended past booms — a credit boom and a sustained rise in the cost of capital — are underway, and reads just 34.
"The meter says there’s a bubble, but it’s not about to burst," Yardeni wrote.
One trigger has kicked in, with the two-year Treasury yield up 115 basis points from its December low, but credit is not stretched outside AI-related areas of the economy. "The preconditions of a bubble are in place and have been for a while, but the forces that ended past booms are only partially present," the firm said.
Yardeni noted that since 1965, quarters with high Conditions and low Triggers readings were followed by an S&P 500 bear market within two years only 9% of the time, with a median inflation-adjusted gain of 18.3% over that period. When both dials read high, the odds of a bear market rose to 42% with a median loss of 12.5%.
"But the Triggers dial is the one to watch: If it starts rising toward High, so do the risks," Yardeni said, flagging the two-year yield and signs of idle capacity in hyperscalers’ third-quarter results as key things to monitor.

Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Bitcoin recovered to around $80,800 on Sunday after a sharp weekend selloff, as investors assessed heavy cryptocurrency liquidations ahead of the Federal Reserve’s upcoming interest rate decision.
The Federal Reserve’s October 27-28 meeting is expected to be a key driver of Bitcoin prices, with traders watching for signals on whether policymakers will maintain interest rates or pursue further tightening.
Higher interest rates could pressure Bitcoin by strengthening the dollar and reducing demand for riskier assets, while a less hawkish outlook could support a recovery.
Elevated oil prices have complicated the outlook, with Brent crude trading above $117 amid the Iran war, raising concerns about persistent inflation.
Bitcoin fell as low as $79,146 on Saturday, its weakest level in more than a month, before reclaiming the psychologically important $80,000 threshold.

According to Fidelity Digital Assets, perpetual preferred stock offerings have financed purchases of approximately 136,000 Bitcoin since 2025.
Companies including Strategy (NASDAQ) and Strive (NASDAQ) have increasingly relied on preferred shares to raise capital, although recurring dividend payments could constrain future purchases.

title: Should Aggregators block AI Agents?
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Online aggregators such as Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Uber Technologies Inc (NYSE:UBER) and DoorDash Inc (NASDAQ:DASH) may be justified in blocking external artificial intelligence agents for now, as the technology threatens to disrupt their business models, according to Bernstein analysts.
In an October 23 research note, the analysts said concerns about AI agents displacing established online platforms may be premature, although the technology could fundamentally reshape how consumers search, shop and transact online.
Dominant aggregators have little incentive to accelerate adoption of competing AI services while developing their own AI-powered experiences.
Amazon has already blocked external agents, prioritising its Alexa shopping ecosystem, while JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have restricted third-party agents over liability concerns.
Successful consumer AI adoption will depend heavily on interoperability, reliability and the ability to complete transactions more conveniently than existing platforms.
Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META) offers an early example of the technology’s potential.
Its Muse AI assistant reached 2.5 million daily active users in North America within six weeks of launch, while 25% of weekly users had tried agentic shopping.
Average purchases exceeded $200, including travel bookings.
Muse has partnered with companies including Walmart Inc (NASDAQ:WMT), Shopify Inc (NASDAQ:SHOP), Instacart (NASDAQ) and Expedia Inc (NASDAQ:EXPE), allowing users to access shopping and travel services.
The research suggests smaller competitors may benefit from partnering with AI agents to gain market share, while dominant platforms face greater risks of losing direct customer relationships.
However, blocking agents is unlikely to remain sustainable if consumers increasingly favour AI-driven transactions.
Platforms with exclusive inventory, established logistics networks and strong customer relationships may have greater flexibility to delay partnerships.
Ultimately, consumer behaviour will determine whether independent AI agents or platform-specific assistants dominate online commerce.
For now, aggregators can reasonably restrict access while assessing adoption trends and negotiating more favourable partnership arrangements.

title: UK immigration crackdown threatens £15 billion care sector - Bloomberg
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
Investing.com -- Britain’s immigration crackdown threatens its £15 billion ($20 billion) care sector, with providers warning of potential business closures, Bloomberg reported Sunday.
Migrant workers account for roughly one-third of Britain’s wider adult care workforce, according to the Work Rights Centre.
Around 280,000 workers entered the country through the Health and Care Visa scheme between February 2022 and July 2025, before the Labour government suspended the route over concerns about abuse.
Under proposed changes, existing visa holders would need to transfer to the Skilled Worker route from July 2028, potentially facing substantially higher salary requirements.
Care providers argue that funding from local authorities is insufficient to support those wages, threatening businesses already struggling with recruitment.
Further uncertainty surrounds Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s proposed settlement reforms, which would extend the standard qualifying period for permanent residency from five to 10 years.
The changes could prevent workers recruited in 2022 and 2023 from securing settlement before their existing visas expire.
Shweta Maulayah, managing director of care provider Maucare, warned that the restrictions could force her to downsize or sell the business.
The sector provides daily support to more than 650,000 vulnerable people, making staffing shortages a significant concern for care providers and local authorities.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is reportedly considering exemptions for care workers, although no final decision has been announced.
The proposals have also faced opposition from Labour lawmakers, with more than 100 parliamentarians previously urging the government to reconsider the reforms.
Some lawmakers want existing migrants protected from retrospective changes and the maximum settlement period limited to seven years.
Care operators say uncertainty is already affecting business decisions, with some exploring sales or closures.
The government is expected to announce further details next month, while providers continue to warn that domestic recruitment remains difficult at current wage levels.

title: Brazil heads to polls in runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr
full_text:
By Oliver Griffin
SAO PAULO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.
The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.
A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro’s 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected.
Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.
Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.
On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds.
Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses.
CANDIDATES ARE NECK AND NECK
Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days.
Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.
The senator’s first-round win sent Brazil’s markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.
His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula.

His candidacy has drawn criticism from Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans, who have alleged links between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood.

title: UAE closes more beaches as Gulf oil spill raises environmental concerns
full_text:
Investing.com -- The United Arab Emirates has expanded beach closures across several northern emirates following an oil spill in the Persian Gulf, raising concerns about environmental damage and potential health risks.
Authorities in Sharjah closed Al Hamriya Beach as a precautionary measure to prevent contamination, while Ras Al Khaimah announced the closure of all its beaches until further notice.
The latest restrictions follow an oil spill detected on Friday off the coast of Umm Al Quwain, north of Dubai.
The UAE’s Ministry of Climate Change and Environment initially ordered the temporary closure of all beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain after identifying the spill.
Authorities have not disclosed the identity of the tanker involved.
The ministry said unusual odours reported in Umm Al Quwain, Sharjah and Ajman did not pose health risks to residents.
Specialised response teams have been deployed to Sharjah to implement protective measures and prevent pollutants from reaching the emirate’s beaches.
The incident adds to a series of maritime pollution events affecting the Gulf region in recent months.
In August, a tanker ran aground near Oman’s southeastern coast, triggering an oil slick covering an area approximately six-and-a-half times the size of Manhattan.
Iran subsequently faced an oil spill near Qeshm Island, close to a breeding habitat for endangered hawksbill sea turtles.
The ongoing regional conflict has further heightened concerns about maritime pollution, particularly around the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier this month, a cargo vessel sank in the strait after an attack triggered a fire, according to Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority.
Other commercial vessels have also been struck by projectiles, raising the risk of fuel leaks and environmental damage even when their main oil storage tanks remain intact.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a critical shipping route for global energy supplies, making maritime safety and environmental protection increasingly important amid continued regional hostilities.

title: Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
full_text:
By Emily Rose and Maayan Lubell
DIMONA, Oct 25 (Reuters) - In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel’s election on Tuesday.
The ballot is Israel’s first since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.
The October 7 security breach saw Likud’s popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.
Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.
"We must have change. Bibi has to go," said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. "Bibi has brought disaster to Israel."
LIKUD LOYALISTS
Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot’s party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls.
It’s a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud.
"I will never betray Likud," said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair.
Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.
Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.
"Most people here vote for Likud just because that’s how they were raised," said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. "The change will come when people start to think about their children’s future rather than their parents’ past."
BATTLE FOR WAVERING LIKUDNIKS
While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can’t be won over, the prize is undecided voters who "understand that we are in a state of crisis" and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot’s Dimona campaign.
Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.
Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.
It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud’s base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute.
A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that "appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud’s traditional electorate", said Asa-El.
In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.
At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.
But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.
"Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love," he said.
Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.
But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel’s youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.
"It’s time for him to go," said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. "He’s done a lot for Israel but it can’t go on. I won’t give my vote to someone almost 80-years-old."

title: Serbia votes as students seek to unseat Vucic in snap election
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
By Ivana Sekularac and Edward McAllister
BELGRADE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Serbia is voting on Sunday as a mass student protest movement seeks to unseat long-time populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade.
The snap parliamentary elections, called by Vucic in September, come after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. The students have since gained widespread support.
Unusually long lines formed at polling stations in Belgrade and Novi Sad before the start of voting at 7 a.m.. Voting ends at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) with first indications of results expected around two hours later.
A student victory would be a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April. It also potentially offers a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
But Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, is a strong incumbent. Many voters thank him for pulling Serbia from economic obscurity and orchestrating a period of sustained modernisation including new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
"I came out early today because the students called us," said Ana, 30, at a polling station in Belgrade.
OPINION POLLS PREDICT TIGHT RACE
Domestically, Vucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, investment in state healthcare and subsidies for young couples. On the international stage, he has balanced closer ties with China, a major investor, and Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, while leaving the door open to joining the European Union.
The students’ domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic.
Opinion polls predict a tight race. In an Ipsos poll published on Thursday, Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is seen leading with 47% of votes versus 40% for the students. But other polls have put the students in the lead.
STUDENT PROTESTS INCREASE PRESSURE ON VUCIC
The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.
Bogdan Pavkovic was one of thousands in central Belgrade for a final student rally on Thursday. He said he wants to change "this awful, horrendous system which cheats on us, which spies on us, which beats us."
Vucic’s office and the Interior Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Vucic and the SNS have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.
"This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns," Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. "We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia."
RELATIONS SOUR WITH EU
Relations with the EU have frayed as the bloc has become increasingly frustrated with Serbia’s lack of reforms over the judiciary, rule of law and corruption.
In a report this month after a visit to Serbia, a delegation from rights body the Council of Europe noted the "hostile and aggressive rhetoric" against opponents.
And in September, EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the huge public funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic held in Belgrade, saying it contradicted “the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union."

title: North Korea’s Kim Jong Un returns from China after war memorial visit, state media says
full_text:
Wells Fargo Names Top Pick Ahead of Q3 Earnings
By Cynthia Kim and Joyce Lee
SEOUL, Oct 25 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un returned from a surprise one-day trip to the Chinese border city of Dandong, where he visited a historic Korean War memorial, North Korean state media said on Sunday.
Kim visited the city on Saturday and returned by road, crossing a newly opened bridge that connects North Korea to its biggest international backer and trading partner. The quick trip symbolised a push by Beijing and Pyongyang to expand trade ties.
North Korean state media emphasised the historical weight of the visit, which came a day before the anniversary of China joining the Korean War on Pyongyang’s side. The bilateral relationship is an "unbreakable" bond forged during the 1950-1953 conflict between North Korea and the US-backed South, state media said.
The two Koreas are technically still at war after the conflict ended in an armistice, rather than a peace treaty.
Kim said during his tour that the North Korean people would "forever remember the glorious years of fighting alongside the Chinese people" and pass down "generational gratitude to the Chinese people who helped our revolution with blood", state news agency KCNA reported.
Beijing and Pyongyang have been seeking to bolster their economic relationship ahead of a trip to the region by US President Donald Trump next month. It also highlights a delicate diplomatic balancing act by Pyongyang, which has also been deepening military ties with Russia in the past two years.
Guided by Wang Huning, the fourth-highest-ranking official in the Chinese Communist Party, Kim visited Dandong’s Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, accompanied by a high-level North Korean delegation that included his sister, Kim Yo Jong, and Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui.
Touring the memorial, Kim viewed an archival photograph of his grandfather, North Korean founder Kim Il Sung, and Mao Zedong, founder of the modern Chinese state, footage from North Korea’s state-run television KRT showed.
Kim presented a commemorative plaque featuring Kim Il Sung as a gift to the museum before holding a formal meeting with Wang and inspecting a bus factory in Dandong.
Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025 for a military parade, and Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June.
"Enjoying a bird’s-eye view at the middle point of the newly inaugurated bridge, Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed expectation that the bridge would undoubtedly and correctly fulfill its historic mission of linking the two countries and firmly joining the minds of the peoples of the two countries," KCNA reported.
